messages.subject: data types and variable declarations
parts:
Hi stan users,

I'm just starting to learn stan and am working my way through the stan reference manual trying to understand data types and declaring/assigning variables. To me, it seems that there are some inconsistencies in the manual and to better understand how the program works I would like to ask three questions (I apologize if these questions are stupid and the result of me not reading the manual properly):

1) In the manual (page 268) there is as an example the following declarations:

vector[5] a[4, 3];
vector[5] b[4];

and then it is stated that the following assignment is legal:
b = a[1];


As I understand it a is declared as an array with two dimensions (4 rows and 3 columns) where each "element" is a vector of length 5 and b is declared as an one-dimensional array of length 4 with elements being vectors of length 5. Further, on the top of page 268 it is described how subarrays can be accessed with less than the full number of indexes. Judging from that description I conclude that a[1] would be a one-dimensional array of length 3 (a has three columns and the elements are 5 element vectors). My questons is then how one can assign a[1] (a one-dimensional array of length 3) to b (which is declared to be a one-dimensional array of length 4)? To me it seems as if the sizes mismatch and hence the assignment should not work.

If it is possible to make such an assignment, what happens to b? Is it turned into a one-dimensional array of 3 or is is still an array of length 4 but with an "empty "element (and which of the elements is then empty?), or what?

2)  I'm having trouble understanding the differences between dimensionality and size/length in the description of arrays.

On page 267 it is said that an array is declared by enclosing its dimensions in square brackets following its name, like in these examples:
int n[5]; // giving an array of 5 integers (I take it this is an one-dimensional array of length 5)
real a[3, 4]; //  giving a two-dimensional array of real values with three rows and four columns i.e two dimensions where the first dimension has size 3 and the second size 4
real <lower=0> z[5, 4, 2]; // three dimensions of sizes 5 by 4 by 2

but then it is said that
vector[7] mu[3]; //gives a three-dimensional array of 7-vectors! -> to me this is an one-dimensional array that has 3 elements (length 3) where each element is a 7 element vector
matrix[7, 2] mu[15, 12] // gives a 15x12-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices -> to me this is a two-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices, it has 15*12 elements arranged in 15 rows and 12 columns where each element is a 7 by 2 matrix

Related to this I have seen examples in the manual where a vector is declared as:
vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;
 Why not use matrix<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;?
Is there any difference? Is corr in the first example a column vector (and how many elements does it have) or a matrix?  

Do I misunderstand all of this or is it not very thourougly (or correctly) described in the manual?

3) As mentoined arrays are declared using square brackets after its name. But, for example, on page 270 one can find the following referred to as a vector:
vector b[4];
To me, this seems to be an array of vectors (of unknown length!). If it is a vector, why is it declared in this way instead of vector[4] b;? Is it OK to declare vectors and matrices where sizes are set using square brackets on their names rather than on the types? Does it make any difference?

I am grateful for any hints on this.

Sincerely
Martin

To me, it seems that there are some inconsistencies in the manual and to better understand how the program works I would like to ask three questions (I apologize if these questions are stupid and the result of me not reading the manual properly):
>
> 1) In the manual (page 268) there is as an example the following declarations:
>
> vector[5] a[4, 3];
> vector[5] b[4];
>
> and then it is stated that the following assignment is legal:
> b = a[1];

> As I understand it a is declared as an array with two dimensions (4 rows and 3 columns) where each "element" is a vector of length 5 and b is declared as an one-dimensional array of length 4 with elements being vectors of length 5. Further, on the top of page 268 it is described how subarrays can be accessed with less than the full number of indexes. Judging from that description I conclude that a[1] would be a one-dimensional array of length 3 (a has three columns and the elements are 5 element vectors). My questons is then how one can assign a[1] (a one-dimensional array of length 3) to b (which is declared to be a one-dimensional array of length 4)? To me it seems as if the sizes mismatch and hence the assignment should not work.

Thanks. It's legal in the language and the program
will compile, but you'd get a runtime error because the
sizes don't match. I'll change for the next release to
declare a as:

vector[5] a[3, 4];

>
> If it is possible to make such an assignment, what happens to b? Is it turned into a one-dimensional array of 3 or is is still an array of length 4 but with an "empty "element (and which of the elements is then empty?), or what?
>
> 2) I'm having trouble understanding the differences between dimensionality and size/length in the description of arrays.
>
> On page 267 it is said that an array is declared by enclosing its dimensions in square brackets following its name, like in these examples:
> int n[5]; // giving an array of 5 integers (I take it this is an one-dimensional array of length 5)
> real a[3, 4]; // giving a two-dimensional array of real values with three rows and four columns i.e two dimensions where the first dimension has size 3 and the second size 4
> real <lower=0> z[5, 4, 2]; // three dimensions of sizes 5 by 4 by 2
>
> but then it is said that
> vector[7] mu[3]; //gives a three-dimensional array of 7-vectors! -> to me this is an one-dimensional array that has 3 elements (length 3) where each element is a 7 element vector
> matrix[7, 2] mu[15, 12] // gives a 15x12-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices -> to me this is a two-dimensional array of 7x2 matrices, it has 15*12 elements arranged in 15 rows and 12 columns where each element is a 7 by 2 matrix

The terminology for these things is a mess. Often
a vector with one dimension of size three will be called
3-dimensional because it represents a point in 3-dimensional
space. I'll try to make this more consistent by saying

> vector[7] mu[3];

is a one-dimensional array of size three holding vectors of size
7.

I tried to stick to "size" rather than "length" (what R uses)
because length is confusable with vector length (e.g., Euclidean).

> Related to this I have seen examples in the manual where a vector is declared as:
> vector<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;
That's a syntax error. It should be matrix.

> Why not use matrix<lower=-1, upper=1>[3,3] corr;?
> Is there any difference? Is corr in the first example a column vector (and how many elements does it have) or a matrix?

There's a chapter in the manual on the various efficiency
tradeoffs of arrays vs. vectors/matrices. Some of the older
examples used arrays where I would've

>
> Do I misunderstand all of this or is it not very thourougly (or correctly) described in the manual?
>
> 3) As mentoined arrays are declared using square brackets after its name. But, for example, on page 270 one can find the following referred to as a vector:
> vector b[4];


> To me, this seems to be an array of vectors (of unknown length!).

If that's what it is, it's illegal. It should be vector[4] b; if it's
a vector or real b[4]; if it's an array. That may have been introduced
when I changed some of the array examples to vectors.

> If it is a vector, why is it declared in this way instead of vector[4] b;? Is it OK to declare vectors and matrices where sizes are set using square brackets on their names rather than on the types? Does it make any difference?
No, only in functions. There's a separate syntax for functions.

>
> I am grateful for any hints on this.

Thanks for reporting. here's the issue which I'll address for the next
release:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2051#issuecomment-247464379

You can report issues directly on GitHub in the currently open
"next manual" issue. Or submit pull requests to fix them. Or just
send to our list like this and I'll transfer them over---we really
appreciate corrections like this.

- Bob
